## 比较的前提：看得见全局

> [强调民族性……要在比较、对照、批判、吸收、升华的基础上，使民族性更加符合当代中国和当今世界的发展要求，越是民族的越是世界的。]{.red}

:::{style="text-align:right"}

--- 习近平《在哲学社会科学工作座谈会上的讲话》（2016年5月17日）

:::

::: {.fragment}

- 比较 &rarr; 需要[可比]{.red}的测量：跨国、跨时、跨调查
- 单国、单题项 &rarr; 结论各执一词
- [鸟瞰视角]{.red}：全球测量 &rarr; 趋势判断 &rarr; 成因检验
- 案例：政治不满情绪，136个国家和地区 [&times;]{.large} 56年 [@MaEtAl2026]

:::

::: {.notes}

开场：讲话强调，学术研究要在"比较、对照、批判、吸收、升华"的基础上推进。比较政治学的核心正是比较，但比较有一个常被忽视的前提：可比的测量。
现实中，大量研究依赖单一国家或单一调查题项，不同数据得出相互矛盾的结论。政治不满是否在上升，至今仍有争论，就是一个典型例子。
"鸟瞰视角"指的是：先把全球、长时段的图景测准，再在这个统一的尺度上判断趋势、检验成因。
今天以政治不满情绪的全球测量与成因溯源为例，说明这条路径怎么走、能回答什么问题。

引文出处：习近平《在哲学社会科学工作座谈会上的讲话》，2016年5月17日；人民网-人民日报2016年5月19日全文。
https://cpc.people.com.cn/n1/2016/0519/c64094-28361550.html
备选（同一讲话，已核对原文）："要按照立足中国、借鉴国外，挖掘历史、把握当代，关怀人类、面向未来的思路，着力构建中国特色哲学社会科学"；"对一切有益的知识体系和研究方法，我们都要研究借鉴，不能采取不加分析、一概排斥的态度。"

:::

## Research Question

Is public discontent with the political system [rising]{.red}? And what [drives]{.red} it?

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center"}

*What I'll offer*

1. A [bird's-eye view]{.red} of political discontent
2. A method for [cross-national, over-time]{.red} comparison
3. A [systematic analysis]{.red} of what drives discontent

:::

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Left: Syntagma Square, Athens, 29 May 2011, about 100,000 people protesting austerity during the debt crisis.
Right: Plaza Baquedano (Plaza Italia), Santiago, 22 October 2019, the estallido social; the flag reads "nos cansamos, nos unimos" (we got tired, we united).
Both are OECD democracies, and both show up in our data: Greece has the second-highest latest discontent score among OECD democracies, and Chile's discontent climbs steadily from the 1990s (see the OECD trends figure later).
Both episodes involved economic grievances, but they are illustrations, not evidence.

[click] Scholars disagree on the most basic fact: is discontent actually increasing?
Foa and Mounk see deconsolidation in developed democracies; Dalton and Jennings et al. document eroding support.
Norris sees trendless fluctuations.

[click] Research question: is discontent rising, and what drives it?

[click] Three promises for the next fifteen minutes.
First, a bird's-eye view: the largest and most temporally and spatially comprehensive dataset on public political discontent to date.
Second, a method: the DCPO latent-variable model, which turns hundreds of incomparable and sparse survey items into comparable country-year estimates.
Third, a systematic analysis: competing explanations (elections, power-sharing institutions, economic conditions) tested together on the same measure for OECD democracies.

Photo sources:
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Greece_Uprising.jpg
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Protestas_en_Chile_20191022_06.jpg

:::


## Why Discontent Matters

- Legitimacy [&rarr;]{.large} democratic survival [@lipset1959some; @miller1974political]
- Discontent [&rarr;]{.large} poor governance [&rarr;]{.large} more discontent [@hetherington1998political]
- Discontent [&rarr;]{.large} [populism]{.red} [&rarr;]{.large} threat to liberal democracy [@mudde2004populist; @urbinati2019political; @doyle2011legitimacy]
- Lens on [backsliding]{.red} and regime stability

::: {.callout-warning}

## Yet the basics remain debated

Nature? Trend? Drivers?

:::

::: {.notes}

Lipset: public belief in a system's legitimacy is essential for democratic survival.
Miller: a democracy cannot endure without majority support; rising discontent raises the potential for revolutionary change.
Hetherington: discontent complicates effective governance, which reinforces dissatisfaction and erodes legitimacy over time.
Discontent also fuels populism, which challenges liberal democracy.
So discontent is a critical lens for predicting democratic erosion and political conflict.

:::

## Why the Debate Persists

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.callout-important}

## Conceptual fragmentation

- Lack of diffuse support [@easton1975re]
- Low responsiveness [@jennings2016dimensions]
- Democratic deficit [@norris2011democratic]
- Incumbent dissatisfaction [@muller1983discontent]

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.callout-warning}

## Data constraints

- [Incomparable]{.red}: different questions, projects, rounds
- [Sparse]{.red}: many country-years never asked
- Different datasets [&rarr;]{.large} conflicting conclusions [@Jennings2017]

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

The debate is largely about how discontent is conceptualized and measured.
Some define it as a lack of diffuse support for the system; others as low responsiveness, democratic deficits, or dissatisfaction with the current government.
The more pressing issue: survey data are incomparable and sparse.
No single question is asked in all countries and years, so researchers rely on different datasets and reach different conclusions.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Our solution**

- [Diffuse support]{.red}: system legitimacy [&rarr;]{.large} threat when eroded

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

*Included*

- External efficacy/responsiveness
- Trust in political institutions
- Perceived political [corruption]{.red}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

*Excluded*

- Trust in incumbent (specific support)
- Support for democracy
- Satisfaction with democracy

:::

::::

:::

::: {.notes}

We follow Easton's distinction. Specific support is satisfaction with incumbent performance; it fluctuates and is not threatening, since citizens can change leaders through elections.
Diffuse support is a "reservoir of favorable attitudes or goodwill"; its erosion gives citizens a normative incentive to seek radical change of the system as a whole.

Included components: low external efficacy (the system is unresponsive), low trust in institutions as a system (parties, politicians, parliament in general), and perceptions of pervasive corruption.

Excluded: trust in the incumbent government (specific support); abstract support for democracy (too prevalent to discriminate, and poorly related to support for actual components of liberal democracy, Hu et al. 2025); satisfaction with democracy (behaves like specific support: winners satisfied, losers not).

<!-- [Suggest] A nested diagram: Easton's political support split into specific vs. diffuse, with the three discontent components under diffuse and the excluded items under specific -->

:::

## Solving the Data Constraints

::::{.overlay-container style="min-height: 480px"}

::: {.overlay-image}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/discontent_Figure_1.png){fig-align="center" height=430}

:::{style="text-align:center"}

[388]{.red} survey datasets &nbsp;|&nbsp; [111]{.red} items &nbsp;|&nbsp; [136]{.red} countries &nbsp;|&nbsp; [56]{.red} years

:::

:::

::: {.overlay-text-over .fragment style="top: 0; transform: translateX(-50%); text-align: left"}

- Solution: Dynamic Comparative Public Opinion [@Solt2020c]
- Output: [PPD scores]{.red}, 3,362 country-years &rarr; publicly available

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Incomparability**

- Difficulty: discontent needed to endorse a response
- Dispersion: noise of each item
- Country-specific bias: translation, culture

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Sparsity**

- Random-walk prior: PPD~t~ = PPD~t-1~ + shock
- Borrows strength across years
- Cost: wider uncertainty in thin years

:::

::::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

We collected 388 survey datasets with relevant questions: 111 distinct items asked in at least five country-years in countries surveyed at least three times.
Coverage: 136 countries and regions, 1968 to 2023, 8,957 country-year-item observations in total.
Left: years of data per country. Upper right: countries with the most year-item observations (UK, US, Sweden). Lower right: number of countries observed per year; coverage takes off in the mid-1990s.
No single question covers all countries and years.

[click] DCPO is a population-level two-parameter ordinal logistic IRT model with country-specific item-bias terms.
Analogy: educational testing. Students take different test forms, yet abilities are placed on a common scale by estimating item parameters.
Each survey question is treated as its own imperfect instrument; differences across instruments are modeled rather than ignored.

Difficulty: "strongly agree" that there is widespread corruption among those who govern expresses more discontent than "strongly agree" that people like me can vote but do nothing else.
Dispersion: how cleanly an item maps onto discontent.
Country-specific bias: same question answered differently across countries.

Sparsity: local-level dynamic linear models within each country; each year equals the previous year plus a random shock.

Result: public political discontent (PPD) scores for all 3,362 country-years spanned by the data, 136 countries and regions, 1968 to 2023. Available on Harvard Dataverse.

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}

| Test | PPD compared with | R |
|---|---|:---:|
| Internal convergent | Source items: cross-section, panel, over time | 0.71 to 0.81 |
| External convergent | Evaluations of democracy, [not]{.red} used in estimation | &minus;0.76 to &minus;0.84 |
| Construct | Government success in health, elderly care, environment | &minus;0.58 to &minus;0.68 |

:::

::: {.notes}

Three tests, one figure each; the table stays on screen.

Internal convergent: PPD vs. the source items used to generate it.
Left: Eurobarometer "tend not to trust" political parties, the single most-asked item (R = 0.74).
Middle: Gallup Voice of the People 2005, "is your country governed by the will of the people?", the most data-rich cross-section (R = 0.71).
Right: Sweden's SOM confidence in parliament, the longest single-country series (R = 0.81).
Correlations account for measurement uncertainty in both measures.

[click] External convergent: items excluded from estimation, evaluations of democracy in one's country (treated as specific support; not every regime identifies with democracy).
ISSP National Identity, proud of how democracy works (R = -0.77); WVS/EVS, satisfied with how democracy is developing (R = -0.84); CSES, satisfied with the way democracy works (R = -0.76).

[click] Construct: discontent should track evaluations of government policy performance.
ISSP Role of Government 2006 and 2016: health care (R = -0.58), the elderly (R = -0.64), the environment (R = -0.68).
Together, the three tests show PPD captures the concept we theorize.

:::

## Hypotheses: What Drives Discontent?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

*Political*

- H<sub>1</sub>: Elections
  - Outlet [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&darr;]{.red}
  - Negative campaigns [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&uarr;]{.blue}
- H<sub>2</sub>: Power-sharing institutions [&rarr;]{.large} inclusion [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&darr;]{.red}

[@lau2007effects; @Kittilson2010; @lijphart1999patterns]

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

*Economic*

- H<sub>3</sub>: Low income, slow growth, unemployment [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&uarr;]{.blue}
- H<sub>4</sub>: Income inequality
  - Grievance [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&uarr;]{.blue}
  - System justification, relative power [&rarr;]{.large} PPD [&darr;]{.red}

[@quaranta2016does; @Jost2019; @Solt2008]

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Elections: discontented citizens can turn dissatisfaction into votes for parties promising change, so PPD should drop in election years. But campaigns also expose citizens to elite and system criticism and misinformation, which could raise PPD.

Institutions: power-sharing systems (parliamentarism, federalism, proportional rules) promote inclusion and send symbolic signals of inclusiveness (Kittilson and Schwindt-Bayer 2010), so citizens should feel more represented and less discontented.

Economy: bad conditions fuel anxiety and anti-establishment sentiment, and citizens use economic indicators to judge system performance.

Inequality: could work like other economic hardship, but system justification theory (the disadvantaged need to defend the system) and relative power theory (the rich shape the attitudes of the poor) predict that rising inequality reduces discontent.

:::

## Research Design

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Data**

- [38]{.red} OECD countries, [1,217]{.red} country-years
- Elections: DES [@Bormann2022]
- Institutions: parliamentarism, federalism, Gallagher index
- Economy: OECD.Stat; Gini: SWIID [@Solt2020]

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Model**

- Bayesian multilevel: country and year intercepts [@Shor2007]
- Within-between: [long run]{.red} vs. [short run]{.red} [@Bell2015]
- Measurement uncertainty in PPD and Gini [@Tai2024]

:::

::::

- Best single item (Eurobarometer) [&rarr;]{.large} 582 obs., Europe only

::: {.notes}

1,217 country-years; 16 (Turkey) to 43 (US) consecutive years per country, mean 32.
The richest single items, Eurobarometer trust in parliament and in parties, each give fewer than half as many observations (582) and exclude the nine non-European OECD members.

Varying intercepts for countries handle heteroskedasticity and allow time-invariant predictors such as federalism; year intercepts capture common time shocks.
Within-between random effects (Bell and Jones 2015): each time-varying predictor is split into its country mean (long-run, historical effect) and the yearly deviation from that mean (short-run effect).
PPD and Gini enter as distributions with known standard deviations, so measurement uncertainty is carried into the estimates. Estimated with brms.

:::

## Results: Economy over Institutions

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/discontent_Figure_6.png){fig-align="center" height=520}

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

- Time trend [&uarr;]{.blue}: rising, not trendless
- Election year [&darr;]{.red}, but modest
- Parliamentarism, federalism: [n.s.]{.grayLight}
- Disproportionality, mean [&uarr;]{.blue}
- Economy: [strongest]{.red} drivers

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Time trend: net of other variables, PPD rises by 0.1 points per year in OECD countries (95% CI: 0.04 to 0.16).
Election years: PPD 0.5 points lower; 95.6% of the posterior below zero. Elections diffuse rather than exacerbate discontent, but a single election is not enough to meaningfully reduce system-level discontent.
Power-sharing: parliamentary or federal systems show no less discontent; short-run changes in disproportionality do nothing. But countries with higher mean disproportionality show more discontent: two SD higher Gallagher index means 3.6 points more PPD (94.9% of posterior positive).

:::

## Long Run vs. Short Run

| Predictor | Long run: between countries | Short run: within country |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| GDP per capita | [&darr;]{.red} | [&darr;]{.grayLight} |
| GDP growth | [n.s.]{.grayLight} | [&darr;]{.red} |
| Unemployment | [&uarr;]{.grayLight} | [&uarr;]{.blue} |
| Income inequality | [n.s.]{.grayLight} | [&darr;]{.red} |
| Disproportionality | [&uarr;]{.blue} | [n.s.]{.grayLight} |

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; color: gray"}

Gray arrow: weak evidence (interval includes zero)

:::

- Bad economy [&rarr;]{.large} discontent [&uarr;]{.blue}, clearest in the short run
- Rising inequality [&rarr;]{.large} discontent [&darr;]{.red}: system justification, relative power

::: {.notes}

GDP per capita: a country 1 SD above the mean has PPD 9.4 points lower than one 1 SD below (95% CI: 14.8 to 4.1). Short run: a 2 SD increase is associated with 0.7 points less discontent (85.6% of posterior negative), so weaker evidence.
GDP growth: no long-run effect; short run, a 2 SD increase yields 1.2 points less discontent (95% CI: 1.8 to 0.6).
Unemployment: long-run estimate 3.9 points (95% CI: -0.8 to 8.5); short run, a 2 SD increase raises discontent immediately by 3.8 points (95% CI: 3.2 to 4.4).
Income inequality: cross-country means show little impact; a 2 SD rise over time lowers PPD by 1.1 points (95% CI: 1.8 to 0.5), as system justification and relative power theories predict.

<!-- [Suggest] A simple two-panel bar chart of the long-run vs. short-run posterior means for the economic predictors would make this contrast more visual than the table -->

:::

## Conclusion

1. Concept: discontent as lack of [diffuse support]{.red}
2. Measure: PPD for [136 countries over 56 years]{.red}, validated three ways
3. Trend: OECD discontent is [rising]{.red}, not trendless fluctuation
4. Drivers: [economic conditions]{.red} matter more than elections and institutions

::: {.callout-important .fragment}

## Contributions

**Theory**: one framework for fragmented measures of discontent<br>
**Method**: comparability [modeled]{.red}, not assumed<br>
**Data**: open panel for backsliding, populism, and regime stability

:::

::: {.notes}

Findings support Foa and Mounk's deconsolidation thesis and challenge Norris's "trendless fluctuations."
Unlike single-country evidence (Jennings et al. 2017), this rests on the most comprehensive cross-national, over-time information available.
Elections relieve discontent only modestly; system-level discontent is not fixed by electoral events alone.
Estimates are associations from observational panel data, not causal effects.

[click] Method: differences across survey items, projects, and countries are estimated in the DCPO model rather than assumed away; sparsity is handled by the dynamic prior, with the cost shown as wider uncertainty.

Data: Harvard Dataverse, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/0II26W; revision history: https://github.com/fsolt/dcpo_discontent

:::

## 鸟瞰视角的启示

1. [概念先行]{.red}：先界定比较什么（扩散性支持 vs. 具体支持），再谈测量
2. [可比性靠建模]{.red}：显式处理题项差异、国别偏差与数据稀疏
3. [全局数据让争论可检验]{.red}：单国、单题项 &rarr; 各执一词；统一尺度 &rarr; 可以裁决
4. 下一步：数据已覆盖非民主政体 &rarr; [跨政体]{.red}比较不满的成因与后果

::: {.fragment}

> [不断推进知识创新、理论创新、方法创新，使中国特色哲学社会科学真正屹立于世界学术之林。]{.red .large}

:::{style="text-align:right; font-size: 0.8em"}

--- 习近平在中国人民大学考察时讲话（2022年4月25日）

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

回到题目：这项研究对比较政治学的意义不只在于"不满是否上升"这一结论，而在于一条可推广的路径。
第一，概念先行。不满的争论很大程度上是概念之争：把对执政者的不满（具体支持）和对体制的不满（扩散性支持）混在一起，结论自然各执一词。
第二，可比性不是假设出来的，而是建模出来的。不同调查、不同题项、不同国家的差异，要在模型里显式估计，稀疏数据的代价也要如实呈现为更宽的不确定性区间。
第三，只有在统一的全局尺度上，"上升还是无趋势"这样的争论才能被检验，而不是停留在各自数据的选择上。
最后，测量覆盖了136个国家和地区，包括非民主政体；成因分析目前只在38个OECD民主国家完成，下一步是把成因检验扩展到全球、比较不同政体下不满的来源与后果。
提醒：组内-组间模型给出的是关联而非严格因果，"成因溯源"是指系统检验各类解释，不是因果识别。

[click] 收尾：回答"世界之问"，前提是看得见世界。全局可比的测量，是中国政治学参与回答世界之问的基础工具之一；也与开场"比较、对照"一句首尾呼应。

## Validation 1: Internal Convergent

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/discontent_Figure_2.png){fig-align="center" height=440}

- PPD vs. source items: cross-section, panel, and over time [&rarr;]{.large} R = 0.71 to 0.81

::: {.notes}

Internal convergent validation compares PPD scores with the individual source items used to generate them.
Left: Eurobarometer "tend not to trust" political parties, the single most-asked item (R = 0.74).
Middle: Gallup Voice of the People 2005, "is your country governed by the will of the people?", the most data-rich cross-section (R = 0.71).
Right: Sweden's SOM confidence in parliament, the longest single-country series (R = 0.81). The dip around 1994 coincides with the turbulence around the EU accession referendum.
Correlations account for measurement uncertainty in both measures.

:::

## Validation 2: External Convergent

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/discontent_Figure_3.png){fig-align="center" height=440}

- Items [not]{.red} used in estimation: evaluations of democracy [&rarr;]{.large} R = &minus;0.76 to &minus;0.84

::: {.notes}

External convergent validation uses items excluded from the estimation: evaluations of democracy in one's country.
We treat them as specific rather than diffuse support, and we do not assume every regime is identified with democracy, so they were excluded from the model.
ISSP National Identity: proud of how democracy works (R = -0.77).
WVS/EVS: satisfied with how democracy is developing (R = -0.84).
CSES: satisfied with the way democracy works (R = -0.76).
Higher discontent goes with lower democratic evaluations, as expected.

:::

## Validation 3: Construct

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/discontent_Figure_4.png){fig-align="center" height=440}

- Government success in health, elderly care, environment [&rarr;]{.large} R = &minus;0.58 to &minus;0.68

::: {.notes}

Construct validation: discontent with the system should be tied to evaluations of recent government policy performance.
ISSP Role of Government 2006 and 2016: perceived government success in providing health care (R = -0.58), providing for the elderly (R = -0.64), and protecting the environment (R = -0.68).
All negative and moderate to strong.
Together, the three tests show PPD captures the concept we theorize and is suitable for analysis.

:::
